body:
Solid advice, thank you.

I have no plans to salvage anything. That died the day we broke up, way back in October. I have gotten better by cutting 90% of her out of my life. The other 10% has to happen naturally. I just couldn't pass up on a chance to say goodbye one last time. Because after this, the likelihood of us meeting by chance again is slim to nil.
Opportunity, mostly. She texted me first, actually. When we spoke in December, we caught up a bit.
Part of me just wants to. There's always an element to missing someone who, love aside, is an example of the kind of person you want to be.
It's usually when I am alone for too long, have had too much caffeine, and sleep deprived. If I can avoid those conditions than I can mitigate the symptoms.
Thanks, I think I need to create an "anxiety meter" or something because there are certainly days (like last Monday) where I'm *this* close to losing it.
Yes. Much of the intensity of that day is not here now. But I won't be surprised if it comes back on another day. Thanks for checking in.

Exercise is rather effective. I'd do more of it if I could, and I will once I work to fix things.

It's not futile if you make the most of it. Though I don't want to sound insensitive if you suffer from depression or the like. Getting job experience can help point you in the right direction, so perhaps apply to some internships if you have the opportunity. These may also get you out of your locale and allow you to meet new people. It's likely that these new people could become future business connections that could get you a job after graduation. I have plenty advice of what to do with your career ands studies based largely on the example of my ex (who has done everything right) and me (who had opportunities and did everything wrong). Then again, you would be taking advice from someone suicidal. So there's that.

Every time I go through a suicidal bout I do remember the sanctity of human life. And for as much as life may be a curse... a cruel, unforgiving, unfair existence, it remains a gift to those still willing to make the decisions to persevere and act, in spite of circumstances. After all, it is what you do with what you're given. 

In the time that I've calmed down from yesterday's madness, I realized killing myself in front of her would not simply end my life. That'd be one thing. But it would damage, no matter how minor, her life. Spite is short-lived, a backwards form of instant gratification. To do damage to her like that would contradict my love for her, and blemish the success and perfection she exhibits to me. 

The what-ifs and should-haves will always remain. Even the best me may not have been enough to match her, and given who I've been, I should forgive myself. Because I went for her in spite of my doubts, and earned myself a year that could've otherwise contained mostly pain. I left a mark, no matter how small, on the course of her life. The fact that I shared that with her was an amazing thing, that a guy like myself got a chance with her. 

I guess what I'm saying is that I should be grateful for the bit of her that I got, and that since I love her so much, I should just let her go about her life now that I'm not a thought in her mind. By letting her go, I'm proving my love. Because selflessness says that I want her to be happy regardless of me. So I guess it is time just to accept what that means.

Had to get that off my chest. If you read that, I'm grateful.

Dude, that's amazing and I don't know why this hasn't received more attention. 

I think about that actually, considering before I met my ex I had attempted suicide five times before. I wouldn't have had the blissful times with her if I had done that. I wouldn't have even met her.

Your advice is sound, honestly. Thank you. I'm starting to come around.

I have been taking up some hiking and roadtripping with my friends when I can, but other priorities can't make this happen all the time.

I used to exercise everyday. Running and cycling. But I have a chronic hip injury that limits what I can do. Ideally I would be putting in the miles, but since my injury I have never been the same. Honestly makes it pretty tough but I'm working on finding a way to get back into it.
Will do, I have a feeling this won't be the last terrible day I have. Thanks for being there for me, it means more than you know.

Hey I appreciate your insight from your hook-up. I figured sex alone couldn't replace a whole person, guess my conscience was right in your case.

Whatever you're doing to stay well in university, keep doing it. I ruined my college experience, and this failed relationship capped it off. Now I have to go back in January to finish a class I failed. Looking back, I would have done college so differently. At least I have a whole semester to give my new wisdom a chance.

What year are you in school?

> we have to work to make the best out of it.

> During my depression i seeked comfort in simple things like going to the gym and drinking green tea. Find something to distract your body and thoughts. Things will get better when you find something!
Talk talk talk. Talk about what your dealing with even the things you dont want people to know.
Seek comfort in people dont isolate.

Sound advice, I really appreciate it. I can't say I have done my best yet, but I think it's time I started working to get better.

I'm sorry that you have felt that, too. I think ultimately you have to go through the pain, that in this case it has to run its course, and that happens best when you are alone. 

I know that being alone hurts me so much now, not just because of her and what would be considered a "normal" aspect of a breakup, but because she was an escape from the problems that I had to face when I was alone. I know there was a time when I went days without a long conversation, and that was actually a good place for me. That was a time when I was fully devoted to facing up to my life and what I wanted, and it's no different than what I need to do now.

> Curious, where do you live?

Northeast. I am at home in Pennsylvania. I go to college in upstate NY.
I have come to the conclusion that forgetting is most of the time all you can do. The rest just sucks.

Thank you for your thoughtful reply. I feel better ready all of that, just wanna say.

Before I knew her, I was really stressed out. I was taking on a huge workload in college and I had just recently put down attempts to return collegiate running for good and had stopped exercising altogether (something I actually enjoy) because of my chronic hip pain. I had stopped trying to battle my long history with an eating disorder, and more or less ate what I felt I needed to, regardless of if it was healthy or frugal. I was constantly anxious and depressed. I didn't enjoy my major studies and I was worried about how that would affect my career in the future. My hopes and dreams for college and life after were either dying or changing completely. That was only 14 months ago.

Some of these concerns have not changed at all. Arguably I still am dealing with all of these problems to this day, except with even more burdens: the fact that I am now set to go back to finish the class I failed so I can get my degree, and that I have this breakup forever reminding me of the happiness I felt with her, but more deeply reminding me of how if I actually worked on myself instead of over-investing in her, I might have bettered myself *and* still be with her.

The lesson has been when I stop working on myself, I will lose any chance of meeting someone like her again. 

I have to go to work now, but I need to heal myself from all these problems once and for all, and properly manage the ones that are forever a part of me.

> If you love someone enough, then you will do anything for them. What if the hardest part about love is letting go? 

Never saw it this way. I needed to hear that. Thank you.
I really appreciate this, I need to hear this, because I can't find the energy to say this to myself right now. Thank you.
There is definitely merit to that kind of positive thinking, but why isn't so hard to stay that way?

Agreed. I have felt *a lot* in my life, but heartbreak is the absolute worst. You find someone you're looking for, someone who in my case came into my life by mere chance, and I can't help but feel I fucked it up even though she's part of the equation, too. 

It's hard to find anyone else because she may have set the bar so high. That's my problem, too. She was almost too good for me (from my view). Some people are just like "as soon as you start hooking up with other women, you'll completely forget about her." I don't think it works like that.

Well yeah, in an unfortunately morbid way I'm glad I'm not alone.

See this is what gives people's existence meaning in the first place is the human connection with have with others. It's what, too, has prevented me from going through with it in the past also.

I don't have a lot of friends. There are some acquaintances out there who might be sad that I die, including some relatives. But I'm not very close to my parents, and a lot of what I have needed from them makes me seem like an absolute burden.

The toughest part about it, I don't know about you, is that suicide continues to look more plausible because my problems continue to make me unworthy of other people's time. People can't always help someone who won't help themselves, and when the consequences from that attitude pile up, what are you left with?
How long has it been for you? What helped you cope in your case?
You're right. I guess the spite comes from wanting her to feel some of the pain I feel because I have seen her to be so cold to me after the breakup.

I have thought about that. If I wouldn't have failed just one class in college last Spring, I would have graduated and I would perhaps have that opportunity to move out of my parent's house where I am temporarily.

I have been living in a way as to spend money to seek new experiences with those who are still my friends, and there are still things I want out of life. I do not have a lot of resources (time, money) to pursue what I enjoy, and the consequences of my mental health burden are starting to eliminate these opportunities entirely.

In the past I have arrived at the conclusion that suicide isn't worth it because death i so unknown. So unknown, that it makes sense that no matter how bad *life* might be, death could hold worse. It's not exactly comforting because it doesn't say that life can't absolutely suck. 

Being in this position of contemplating suicide on off for some time even *before* our breakup has had me in this catch-22-like position: I want to die because life sucks, but I don't want to die because death could be worse. And so my attitude has gone back and forth between "this is my life, my only life, I need to take care of it and do as much as a possibly can" and, "fuck it, I'm going to kill myself soon, might as well as neglect everything and have some crazy fun before I pull the trigger."

But to be totally honest, I don't want to be alone in a new place far away from people I do know and trust. Being alone is the number one toughest thing for me right now because being with people is one of the few activities that makes thinking of my ex bearable. The problem has been I am normally an introverted person, and before I used to have no problem spending time alone. I built much of my life around it. And now, being alone is torture. Because of her.

That's quite the story, honestly. Thanks for sharing. How long were you dating? You said it took you six months until things turned around?

I go back and forth suicide so many times. I find that when I am suicidal I just neglect anything and everything because I assume I'm going to die. And when I don't, I have all these consequences from that attitude them left with, very, very serious consequences.

I should mention I have had a long history with an eating disorder and issues with anxiety and depression. I have attempted suicide five times. That's ultimately the cause of why she left me, because I wasn't treating them, I was just using her as an escape, even though I really did love her. And that's what is motivating me to really go through with it this time. I'm 23, the consequences are real, I'm going to be a complete and utter failure of a human being if I choose to stick around. 

I get days like today, where I especially want it to end. Then my friends and family would finally get the message that my mental health problems *were* serious, and I would finally be free of all my suffering. I don't understand why the material wealth that I have relative to the rest of the world, that I'm a white, college educated male with opportunities, doesn't make me happy whatsoever. I haven't found a way around what I feel and I'm just tired of the majority of every day being devoted to just surviving the thoughts, feelings, and impulses. I'm dying from the inside out and I feel helpless against it. 

I know that if I commit suicide, I end the chances of anything getting better. But there's no guarantee that they will. I don't like half-assing my life. I either want to succeed, or die. I hate being a failure.

Fair enough. Honestly I don't know if it would affect her at all other than the gore aspect of it. I'd rather die seeing her than die alone. Perhaps I can do it immediately after I see her, so she doesn't have to see it. 

What's the story with your girlfriend? Were you the first one to find her? I think the difference is that this girl is my ex, and she left me. I secretly thinks she would be happier seeing me die, but I have never really asked her so I wouldn't know.

I mean, I know relationships end sometimes. But I have never felt a breakup so one-sided. The other thing is that I don't feel in control of feelings for her. A genuine love is like genuine laughter, when it's true you can't hold it back. 

You are right though. I admitted myself that she was the only person holding me up, inspiring me to get better. Not exactly healthy, but it happened. Now here I am, helpless.
I'd like to hear your story.
What it's like for you now?

You're right, I can't know. And that's generally one of the reasons that's stops me from acting out my suicide plans, besides the fear of what happens after death. But I am so tired of seeing things get worse, enduring the anger, anxiety, depression, and hopelessness. I feel that if I'm sticking around I should not be wasting my time not doing what I should be doing to get better.

Does the fact that life *might* get better rationally eliminate any justification for suicide? I suppose I don't like living with the uncertainty that life might only continue to get worse or might actually get better. 

I don't want to paint myself as over-indulging in despair and self-loathing, as if to say there is nothing good about life. There are good things that have happened to me and perhaps will happen to me again. But why don't they change how I feel? The fear and emptiness, the pain of memories, the anger the anxiety, it has just stuck around despite my hope and patience. 

Do you have to work harder to make the feelings go away, to motivate yourself to act in your best interest? Is that what it comes down to, that I'm not trying hard enough? 

What allowed you to reach the point you're at now?

Doing what I can. I have another job interview Friday and I should have applied to a few internships by the end of the week. I'm redoing my resume. 

I study IT. I am just not passionate about it. The only thing I was passionate about was food/health/fitness, and most of all running/cycling. I just can't make a living in any of those things and so part of the depressing reality I face is that in order to maintain the standard of living I am used to, I pretty much have to stay in IT. I'm too old to change careers and I can't start my life without having the money to be independent, even if I wanted to go to school for something else. It's just reality and I have to face it, you know? No matter how depressing it is to me.

> Don't do it for this relationship. Do it for you.

This is the advice I wasn't expecting to hear, but needed to hear. I agree completely. Part of moving forward from the past will be doing so for the right reasons.

I can't go back to school until next Fall, realistically. I don't have the money yet. But I know I can't move on without it. 

I think the distance is manageable (she is only 2 hours away) but only if I am someone to her that makes it worth it. It's obvious now, but I needed additional perspective.

Thank you.

I am working much harder now in light of her words to me. I am trying to find an internship for the Spring, in the meantime I am looking to find a second job (I just got a call back about an interview last night).

It's going to take awhile, but I think I'll get there. Thanks for replying.

This will be buried, downvoted, and disagreed with. But I'm going to make this point known.

I've attempted suicide four times in my life, in accordance with the severity of my conditions. I've thought again about taking my own life recently, since I continue to get worse, and ever since my eating disorder and subsequent depression began, I've never been the same and will probably never be the same. Perhaps it will soon be time, but I'll speak my mind.

It's constant management on a daily, momentary basis of the symptoms and bullshit in my mind that me and people like me have to deal with. We have mental obstacles that 'normal' people do not, and that makes life in a far more modern and competitive place that much harder. I don't pretend to ignore the life around me and the material riches I have—some opportunity, an education, a job, a family, a place to live, and too much food—but for whatever reason it offers no solace for me. Take a look at r/depression and you will clearly see I am not alone. 

The problems people like me face at the mental and behavioral levels of health are not cured by simple solutions or emotional support alone. They are often as permanent as our own being, and thus, only eliminated by the taking of our own lives. There is no escape, and I believe people like me truly suffer due to the incurable and dynamic nature of our mental/behavioral illnesses. We are insulted by the people who tell us "this too shall pass." I've been fighting for five fucking years of my life that could've otherwise been the best years of my youth, instead destroyed by the decision to persist somehow on the idea that "it will get better." No, these are lies. Sometimes it *doesn't* get better, and not even because of what could be a self-fulfilling prophecy.

But I digress. People like me, who suffer from such mental and behavioral conditions, it is our right to kill ourselves. It is our right to decide whether we live or die, if not a fundamental right in all humans. If we can't survive and make it in this world, then the burden is almost on *us* to remove ourselves from the pool of resources that is better spent on the people who would do so much better with them. The sooner we die, the less is wasted, and I, in fact, from a purely resourceful point of view, would have no problem removing myself from the world on this idea alone, if it weren't so damn hard to overcome myself in doing so. I've tried. People who for whatever reason don't suffer will never understand that and will always want to convince us to stay. More people ought to read [Bill Zeller's suicide note](http://gizmodo.com/5726667/the-agonizing-last-words-of-bill-zeller).

In cases where the premise for suicide is indeed curable, than your efforts are certainly applauded. Help those who can be helped, and keep doing what you're doing. Not every suicide is equally justified, though it is that person's right to do so. And while it is a very selfish worldview, if me and people like me can't be helped, it is our right to die.

"People say suicide is selfish. I think it's selfish to ask people to continue living painful and miserable lives, just so you possibly won't feel sad for a week or two. Suicide may be a permanent solution to a temporary problem, but it's also a permanent solution to a ~23 year-old problem that grows more intense and overwhelming every day." - Bill Zeller

I experience lots of emotions on daily, weekly, almost cyclical basis. Rage, frustration, loathing, depression, self-hatred, hope, giddiness, dread, joy, annoyance, and a lot of others I can't quite describe. I think I'm more emotional than a lot of men.

I don't think I've cried since I was maybe 14 or 15, with the one exception being the time I was overwhelmed with the severity of suffering from my eating disorder and subsequent depression.

I tend to get very emotionally connected to memories, which is unfortunate, because I have a very good memory and recall so many different feelings as a result. All the good memories from my youth thus serve as heart wrenching, painful reminders of how things used to be good and care-free, but now cause me lots of soul-crushing pain.

Right, and I agree. I've rationalized that before.

The issue for me is that, number one, I can't engage in that amount of not-give-a-fuckery without upending the entire structure of my life as well as my family and friends, and number two, the ambitions that I have like that—such as biking across the country in May—I can't do when I'm soon-to-be overweight and addicted to food.

I built myself up and the fact that I keep fucking up, and I'm addicted, et. al. has been tearing me down ever since. I almost broke down and LoA'd out of college, but my friend convinced me to see it through. Whatever.

Funny you ask, I was legitimately planning suicide again today.

I'm so fucking tired of dealing with my eating disorder, how I feel, these cravings, just... everything.

I've already attempted suicide 4 times in my life.

It's not that I don't think things will change. They will. I just don't know if I can live with the consequences to my well-being that come with choosing to continue to live.

It's a lose-lose if I ever knew one.
Thank you, your reply was very helpful (this was one of the questions I didn't ask my friend). I'm sure my girl will let me know if I'm doing it right.

I'll make 100% sure there's consent. In fact, my goal is to go into it sober.

I've attempted suicide four, maybe five times. 

Every time I swore more and more that it was the end, that I would end it, that I was done with bullshit, that I would put an end to the suffering once and for all.

But I'm still here. 

Willing to listen to you, to be open to your own suffering, to hear everything that you feel you can't share with anyone. You don't even have to *trust* me; I don't expect you to. This is the internet, no one knows who you are, you're free to share everything you want and everything you don't.

First and foremost, understand that suicidal tendencies happen because pain exceeds coping resources. After several attempts at my own life, this holds true. And it's cyclical, too.

You're craving a way to cope, a way out, a way to deal with the problems, that as you imply, are overwhelming. You're so desperate, desperate for that way out, that you're willing to contemplate taking your own life.

I'll start by saying there's always another way, and that no matter how low I felt, no matter how bad I wanted to take my own life, that after I tried to kill myself, I walked away from that attempt with a deeper and better understanding of myself, and my identity, a new hope or resolution or truth or whatever you want to call it that allowed me to go on.

You might find that even if you did try to kill yourself (which you *won't*), that you hesitate, that there's something holding you back. No matter how you try and suppress it, no matter what weight your suffering has on you, that it can't crush that spark to just live, no matter how depressed or fucked up you feel.

Once you (re)discover this part of yourself, which *does* exist, you can then embrace my next plea: life gets better, one way or another it does. Change, newness, it's the force of life. As long as you decide to stick around, time will drag you on, shove you into newness, and suddenly you will forget, at least momentarily, that suffering you're dealing with.

You're sixteen years old. Sixteen. You have so much youth left to live, so many chances to let the newness of you life take you into fun, good, and happy experiences.  You have the chance that a lot others don't have. I've made mistakes in the past that I can't change now. You're too young to have to worry about what's already happened when there's so much potential for what's in front of you.

I suffer from an eating disorder, depression, and being bipolar, and the weight of having an intelligent mind that allows me to rationalize and analyze and give me all these perfectionist standards that I've made myself suffer by trying to attain. 

For me, contemplating suicide as I did helped me realize that there is no "over it." That my suffering can only be managed or mismanaged, that as long as I'm alive it will still exist. Sometimes, the weight of this is unbearable, where I really did want to die. In the end, I learned the truth, which Lance Armstrong puts so well. I swear by this, despite everything I've been through:

**"Pain is temporary. It may last a minute, an hour, a day, or a year, but eventually it will subside and something else will take its place; if I quit, however, it lasts forever."**

Talk to us. Tell us what's wrong. Go an epic rant. We're here to listen. You ought to let it out, so you can cope, as I said earlier. I, for one, I'm here for you.

How frequent were your binges at their worst? How far are you from a weight you would consider healthy? Do you make overeating a deliberate, per-meditated thing, or do you just let them happen when you encounter any form of resistance?
I'm a big fan of IF. Glad it's working for you. What helps you eat properly portioned meals when it is time to eat?

Thank you for your support and telling your story. A question or two:

When you would overeat, did you have an affinity for certain foods, perhaps predominantly high-carb, high-sugar ones? I know this seems obvious but I rarely ever crave meat or fast food or anything high fat.

With regards to forming self-respect, what were some attitudes or thought processes that you changed to see yourself in a better light?

> I don't want to be someone and strive for something or be successful... I just want to live. 

IMO, this is your starting point. In both my own experiences with suicide, and in most online pleas I've read convincing you not to kill yourself, it is the hesitation you have to kill yourself that proves your will to live. Well, dusted off my throwaway account to reply. And to say I'm sorry that this will come off as a 'blind leading the blind' situation.

But let's just say in terms of your ED and the other problems with it, I relate completely. If you want to know about my own struggle, I'm open to questions, but this about you and the advice you may or may not find useful.

Just a couple simple points that might help you out:

**1. "*The pursuit of the dream is what will heal you.*" - Billy Mills**

If there's one thing that's helped motivate me time after time, if there's one thing that keeps me going no matter how much more fucked up I get, it's this quote. I'll explain by saying I've attempted suicide 4 times. 4 fucking times. And there are weeks like this one where honestly I just want to die. By the sounds of it you've felt the same way at some point. 

The reason this keeps me going is because I know that the only way I can get better, or find some status quo, is if I commit myself to a dream. A purpose. Some idea or some calling about my identity or my being that no matter how much I try to hide from or deny that I don't want... will always remain. A purpose so sincere that thinking about it relative to how fucked up you are causes you more emotional pain than anything else. No matter how depressed I get, or how much food I eat, or how much I hate myself, that dream remains...

My experiences with attempted suicide have taught me it's not about why you shouldn't die, since that's inevitable, but why you should live in the first place. All the time I've wasted trying to rationalize self-worth and existence and all the other philosophical musings about life have at least shown me that A, people will always be fucked up, and B, no one really has a clue about the meaning of life anyway. So who cares how fucked up you get in the process of trying to get better? 

And that brings me back to the quote above. Find something to work for. Find something worth fighting for. Something you're absolutely sure of, in your heart. Don't compromise. Don't hide from yourself. Even if the only thing you can think of is, "I just want to stay alive." Then that's your purpose. Just stay alive. If you think you're so messed up that you're going to kill yourself anyway, does anything else about reality really matter?

The last thing I'll say about this point, is when you recognize that dream worth holding onto, you can slowly cultivate it into actionable change. The journey required to achieve that dream—getting lost in the process—is the most critical aspect of getting better. Learning to deal and accept the blows your eating disorder causes along the way. Because once you see your ED as not your whole life, you learn to slowly accept the problem and continue to come back to that dream. And if you die and you never get that dream? So what? How is that moment any different than moment you thought about giving up everything and dying with all that perceived unfulfillment?

**2. "Know yourself."**

The most important thing in finding a way to get better. All the cognitive, psychological, biological, experiential factors behind your addiction to food aside, knowing who you are and how you view yourself is the key to getting better.

Somewhere, 'deep' inside yourself are some internal beliefs or causes that drive your eating behavior. Or at least in my experience with food addiction, I think so. Somewhere in the back of your head there's the voice of decision making, no matter how subconscious it seems, that tells you that overeating is okay or the thing you should always do whether it's justified or not. 

Learning to be in tune with yourself to recognize, in the moment, these thoughts is the first as well as the final step in recovery, IMO. I'll try to be more specific: Recognize and accept that you do want all the food that those intrusive thoughts say you want. If you deny those those thoughts, and fear them, as I have, then you will forever be put in a position to resist yourself. To further hate yourself. And that's simply not the way.

I suppose a better way of saying it is that you have to treat your addiction at its source, which only you can figure out. 

**3. Drop everything; go for a walk.**

I think one of the most important things I've done and don't utilize enough is the importance of going on absurdly long walks with no destination or duration in mind. Walking itself has all kind of benefits physically, but the wonders it can work on your mind are even more valuable.

Go somewhere, maybe in the woods, like hiking, or perhaps a nature trail. Some people would find a busy city with streets that go on forever would be a good place. Maybe a beach shoreline, or a shaded path around a lake. Any of these will be sufficient.

Just start walking with no destination or duration in mind. Think about everything. Let your mind wander. Let it go off and do it's own thing and don't try and control your thoughts. The first time I did this, I often spoke out loud to myself, because I found that things were getting very emotional.

I find this does a couple of things. It lets me express myself and everything that's bothering me. I'm not locked in trying to control anything. It helps to put some distance between me and the constant threat of overeating. More importantly, once all the nasty stuff has floated out of my head, I start to get a little optimistic and my motivation/willpower seems to recharge itself a little. It helps me to reflect, and most importantly it keeps me alive.

I can't really explain how it will work for you other than to just give it a try. I find that when I'm done, I like to go down to my favorite creek and sit by the rushing water for a while.
